chapter_title: Smart Contract Testing with Hardhat and Waffle

screens.title: Smart Contract Testing with Hardhat and Waffle
screens.subtitle: Build a fast, reliable local test environment and write tests that find bugs before deployment

narration.text: Testing smart contracts is not optional. In this chapter you will learn how to set up Hardhat and Waffle to run fast, local tests that exercise contract logic, events, and Ether flows. We emphasize concrete test patterns: isolated unit tests, multi-account scenarios using signers, assertions for reverts and events, and tests that simulate attacks like reentrancy. You will see a simple Counter contract and a test suite that checks initial state, state changes, cross-account interactions, and expected failures. The practical benefit is immediate: tests provide a rapid feedback loop so you can catch logic errors, access-control gaps, and gas-related issues before contracts touch a live network. Along the way we’ll adopt test-driven development habits that help you design safer, smaller functions and clearer APIs. By the end of this lesson you will be able to initialize a Hardhat project, write Waffle-enhanced Chai assertions for events and balance changes, and craft tests that assert security properties. Think of testing as your safety net: it lets you experiment confidently and prevents costly mistakes in production. What failure would you rather find locally than on a mainnet transaction?

keyIdea.title: Why testing matters
keyIdea.text: Tests detect logic bugs, validate security properties, and provide a fast feedback loop that prevents costly production errors.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives will guide your practice as you learn Hardhat and Waffle. First, you will be able to initialize and configure a Hardhat project so you have a private local network and a reproducible toolchain. Second, you will write comprehensive unit tests that exercise contract logic, state transitions, and emitted events using Mocha and Chai extended by Waffle matchers. Third, you will simulate transactions from different accounts and with different Ether values using signers to verify access controls and balance changes. Finally, you will design tests aimed at common vulnerabilities such as reentrancy and denial-of-service, and apply test-driven development to iteratively design safer contracts. Each objective is practical: for example, configuring Hardhat ensures your test runs are fast and repeatable, while writing an event assertion guarantees off-chain listeners can trust on-chain signals. Keep these goals visible as you write tests: they help you prioritize edge cases and failure modes, not just the happy path. Which objective will change how you write your next contract?

narration.text: This second set of objectives focuses on applied testing skills you will use in the hands-on activity. You will practice writing tests that intentionally trigger and assert reverts, verifying that access control modifiers prevent unauthorized actions. You will also assert event emissions to ensure external systems can rely on your contract signals. Another objective is to measure side effects: use Ether balance assertions to confirm net transfers while accounting for gas. Finally, you will learn how to simulate Denial-of-Service scenarios and large inputs to validate gas-resilience or batching strategies. Each objective is practical: for instance, asserting an event prevents subtle bugs in off-chain indexing, and testing reverts guards against privilege escalation. As you practice, adopt the habit of testing both the happy path and failure paths. This mindset change is often the biggest step toward secure contract development. screens.title: Why tests are essential for smart contracts
screens.subtitle: From deterministic local runs to security validation

narration.text: Start with a clear claim: smart contract testing is essential because contracts are immutable once deployed and mistakes are costly. A good test suite gives you deterministic, repeatable checks that can exercise both correct behavior and attacker strategies. Practically, Hardhat provides a local Ethereum network so each test run is fast and isolated; you can reset state between tests or deploy fresh instances in a before-each hook. Waffle extends Chai with matchers tailored to contract interactions, letting you assert events, reverts, and Ether balance changes expressively. Concrete example: writing a test that asserts a withdraw function emits a FundsWithdrawn event with the beneficiary address and updates the beneficiary balance gives you two independent checks — an on-chain signal and the actual Ether flow. A common misconception is that unit tests alone are enough; they are necessary but must be complemented by integration tests and scenario tests that simulate multiple contracts and edge cases. Another misconception is relying only on console output during tests; assertions are the durable, automatable artifact. Key takeaway: think of tests as executable documentation that proves both behavior and security properties. What small but critical assertion will you add to your next test?

keyIdea.title: Testing claim
keyIdea.text: Tests are the primary defense against costly, irreversible errors in deployed smart contracts.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Why testing matters
Definition & claim

A test suite provides deterministic checks against contract logic and security properties before deployment. With Hardhat’s local network, you run tests quickly without relying on public testnets.

Example
Assert that a withdrawal emits a FundsWithdrawn event and increases the beneficiary's Ether balance.
Misconception
Passing the happy path does not guarantee safety; tests must include reverts, edge cases, and adversarial scenarios.
Key Takeaway

Treat tests as executable specifications that prove both functionality and security properties.

Practical checklist
  • Run assertions for both state change and emitted events.
  • Use fresh deployments for isolated tests with beforeEach.
  • Simulate transactions from different signers to test access control.
  • Create adversarial contracts for reentrancy and DoS tests.
Try this
Add one failing test that demonstrates an expected revert, then implement the fix and make it pass.

screens.title: Project setup: install Hardhat and Waffle
screens.subtitle: Install dependencies and initialize a basic Hardhat project

narration.text: Setting up a reliable test environment starts with the toolchain. Install the development dependencies for Hardhat, Waffle, Ethers, and Chai so you can compile, deploy, and assert contract behavior locally. After installing node and a package manager, create a project folder, initialize a package manifest, and install the listed dev dependencies. Then initialize Hardhat; choose the basic sample project or an empty config depending on your preference. The Hardhat configuration file specifies the Solidity compiler version and any network overrides for local testing. A concrete example of a minimal configuration includes the solidity version used by your contracts. A common mistake is leaving mismatched compiler versions between your config and contracts; this can cause unexpected compilation errors. Another practical tip is to save the exact dependency versions to package. json so CI tests remain reproducible. After this setup you will have contracts and test directories ready to receive code and test files. When you're ready, run the local test command to ensure the environment is operational and repeatable. screens.title: A simple contract to test: Counter.sol
screens.subtitle: A minimal contract to demonstrate state tests and reverts

narration.text: We use a simple Counter contract to focus on test patterns instead of complex business logic. The contract exposes a public count, increment and decrement functions, and a getter. Using Solidity 0.8. x makes arithmetic safe by default, which changes how you write underflow tests compared to older compiler versions. For example, if you attempt to decrement below zero, Solidity 0.8. x will revert automatically. In tests you assert that the decrement call reverts when count is zero. This contract also highlights multi-signer interactions: different accounts can call increment and the global count reflects those calls. A common misconception is that simple contracts don’t need tests; in reality, they make excellent examples for asserting state transitions, reverts, cross-account behavior, and event emission in more complex contracts. When you test this contract, write tests for initial state, increment and decrement behavior, reverts on underflow, and multi-account interactions to practice connect patterns. Once comfortable, the same patterns scale to larger, security-critical contracts. A simple contract to test: Counter.sol means use simple contracts to practice state assertions, revert checks, and multi-signer interactions before testing complex systems.. In practical terms, a minimal contract to demonstrate state tests and reverts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test subject
keyIdea.text: Use simple contracts to practice state assertions, revert checks, and multi-signer interactions before testing complex systems.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Counter contract
Counter.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Counter {
    uint256 public count;

    function increment() public {
        count++;
    }

    function decrement() public {
        count--; // Solidity 0.8.0+ reverts on underflow
    }

    function getCount() public view returns (uint256) {
        return count;
    }
}
This contract demonstrates state mutation, safe arithmetic in modern Solidity, and a simple getter. Tests should assert both state values and revert behavior for invalid operations.
Testing focus areas
  • Initial state equals zero.
  • Increment increases the count by one.
  • Decrement reverts when count is zero.
  • Different signers can interact with the contract via connect.
Key Takeaway
A minimal contract helps you focus on test structure, assertions, and attacker simulation before applying the patterns to larger contracts.

screens.title: Test structure with Mocha and Waffle
screens.subtitle: Organize tests using describe, beforeEach, and it blocks

narration.text: A well-structured test file reads like a specification. Use describe to group related tests, beforeEach to set up a fresh contract deployment and signers, and it blocks to state individual assertions. In the setup you obtain signers from the local Hardhat network and deploy a fresh contract instance. This pattern prevents state leakage between tests and keeps each it block focused on one behavior. For example, the beforeEach hook retrieves three signers, deploys the Counter contract, and ensures the contract is ready to test. A common mistake is deploying once for all tests instead of deploying before each test; that can make tests order-dependent and hide stateful bugs. Another tip: keep each it block short and assert one observable property, such as a state value, emitted event, or revert. When you sequence tests this way, test failures point directly to the broken behavior and are easier to fix. How might you refactor a fragile test suite into isolated, reliable cases? Test structure with Mocha and Waffle means use beforeeach and fresh deployments to avoid cross-test state contamination and keep tests deterministic.. In practical terms, organize tests using describe, beforeeach, and it blocks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test hygiene
keyIdea.text: Use beforeEach and fresh deployments to avoid cross-test state contamination and keep tests deterministic.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Test structure
Test skeleton
const { expect } = require("chai");
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

describe("Counter", function () {
  let counter, owner, addr1, addr2;

  beforeEach(async function () {
    [owner, addr1, addr2] = await ethers.getSigners();
    const Counter = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter");
    counter = await Counter.deploy();
    await counter.deployed();
  });

  it("should have initial count of 0", async function () {
    expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(0);
  });
});
This skeleton shows the standard pattern: retrieve signers, deploy the contract, and write short, focused it blocks for assertions.
Practical tips
  • Prefer fresh deployments in beforeEach for isolation.
  • Keep each test focused on a single observable outcome.
  • Use clear, descriptive test names that explain expected behavior.
Common mistake
Reusing the same contract across tests can hide stateful bugs and make failures dependent on earlier tests.

screens.title: Writing concrete Counter tests
screens.subtitle: Initial state, increment, decrement, and revert cases

narration.text: Let’s walk through concrete tests that validate Counter behavior. Start with an initial-state test asserting the getter returns zero. Next, test increment by calling the increment function and asserting the count increases by one. For decrement, create a small sequence: increment once, then call decrement, and verify the count returns to zero. For the underflow test, attempt to call decrement when the count is zero and assert that the call reverts. In Solidity 0.8. x this underflow reverts automatically, so your test should use a reverted assertion. A concrete example is asserting that the decrement call is reverted without relying on specific error text, which keeps the test compatible with native arithmetic checks. A common pitfall is writing tests that assume gas-free operations; always expect gas costs and avoid asserting raw transaction costs unless you're intentionally testing gas impact. After these tests run, your test suite gives you confidence in basic state transitions and failure behavior, and you’re ready to extend tests to multi-signer interactions. Writing concrete Counter tests means assert both successful state changes and expected reverts to validate both happy paths and failure modes.. In practical terms, initial state, increment, decrement, and revert cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Concrete checks
keyIdea.text: Assert both successful state changes and expected reverts to validate both happy paths and failure modes.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Counter tests
Test examples
it("Should have an initial count of 0", async function () {
  expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(0);
});

it("Should increment the count", async function () {
  await counter.increment();
  expect(await counter.getCount()).to.equal(1);
});

it("Should revert on underflow if count is 0", async function () {
  await expect(counter.decrement()).to.be.reverted;
});
These short tests provide clear, deterministic checks of behavior. The reverted check proves the contract prevents invalid arithmetic underflow in modern Solidity.
Example scenario
A developer introduces a change to decrement that bypasses safety checks. These tests would immediately fail on the underflow case and point to the change, catching a regression before deployment.
Key Takeaway
Short, focused tests reduce debugging time and provide a clear signal when behavior changes unexpectedly.

screens.title: Signers and connect(): simulating multiple accounts
screens.subtitle: Use signers from Ethers.js to test access control and cross-account interactions

narration.text: Signers are objects that represent accounts and let you send transactions from different addresses in tests. In Hardhat, you obtain signers via the provider and use connect on a contract instance to simulate a call from a specific account. For example, to verify that a function is restricted to an owner, deploy the contract with the default signer, then connect the contract instance to a second signer and assert the call reverts. This pattern is essential for access-control tests and multi-user scenarios like contributions or token transfers. A concrete code pattern is retrieving three signers during setup and using the second signer to call a protected function and expect a revert with the proper message. A common misconception is that calling a function with different sender addresses requires separate deployments; connect provides a simple, per-call way to change the originating signer. Key takeaway: always include at least one test that asserts a privileged action fails for a non-authorized signer. That one test often prevents privilege escalation bugs from reaching production. Signers and connect(): simulating multiple accounts means use signers and connect to simulate transactions from multiple accounts and validate access control and multi-user logic.. In practical terms, use signers from ethers.js to test access control and cross-account interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Signers role
keyIdea.text: Use signers and connect to simulate transactions from multiple accounts and validate access control and multi-user logic.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Signers & connect
Pattern
Get signers in beforeEach, then call contract.connect(signer).functionName(...) to simulate a transaction from that account. Use this to test onlyOwner modifiers and multi-user interactions.
Example
After deploying as owner, use connect with addr1 and expect a protected call to revert with the correct message.
Why it matters
  • Verifies access control and authorizations.
  • Simulates user roles without redeploying contracts.
  • Supports realistic multi-account scenarios for economic flows.
Misconception
Assuming the deployer is always the caller hides many authorization bugs; explicitly test non-deployer callers.

screens.title: Asserting events and Ether balance changes
screens.subtitle: Use Waffle matchers to validate off-chain signals and net transfers

narration.text: Events and Ether balance assertions are crucial for verifying side effects that off-chain services rely upon. Waffle adds matchers that let you assert an event was emitted with exact arguments and check the net Ether balance change of an account after a transaction. For example, when testing a withdrawal, assert that the contract emitted a FundsWithdrawn event with the beneficiary address and correct amount, and also assert the beneficiary's balance increased by that amount net of gas costs. The changeEtherBalance matcher handles gas costs by checking net changes rather than raw transfer values. A common error is assuming event presence equals correct state change; always assert both the event and the resulting state or balance. As a practical example, write a test that deposits Ether into a contract, calls withdraw, asserts the event, and uses changeEtherBalance to check the recipient's net gain. These paired assertions catch mismatches between logs and actual value transfers. Asserting events and Ether balance changes means assert events and net ether balance changes to validate both on-chain signals and actual value flows.. In practical terms, use waffle matchers to validate off-chain signals and net transfers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Side-effect checks
keyIdea.text: Assert events and net Ether balance changes to validate both on-chain signals and actual value flows.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Events & balances
Event assertion example
await expect(token.transfer(addr1.address, 100))
  .to.emit(token, "Transfer")
  .withArgs(owner.address, addr1.address, 100);
This test ensures the Transfer event was emitted with the correct arguments, which off-chain indexers depend on.
Balance change example
await myContract.deposit({ value: ethers.utils.parseEther("1.0") });
await expect(() => myContract.withdraw(ethers.utils.parseEther("0.5")))
  .to.changeEtherBalance(owner, ethers.utils.parseEther("0.5"));
Use changeEtherBalance to assert net changes while letting the matcher account for gas costs. Pair this with an event assertion for completeness.
Key Takeaway
Combine event and balance assertions to fully validate side effects that matter to users and integrations.

screens.title: Testing for reentrancy and DoS
screens.subtitle: Design adversarial tests that attempt to break your contract

narration.text: Testing for vulnerabilities means writing tests that try to break your contract in realistic ways. For reentrancy, deploy a malicious attacker contract inside the test suite that calls into the victim contract’s vulnerable function and attempts to re-enter before state updates complete. The test should set up the victim with a balance, execute the attack, and then assert whether the victim’s balance or state was drained. If it was, the test proves a vulnerability exists; if it was not, the test proves the defense works. For Denial-of-Service, create tests that populate a contract with many participants or call functions with large inputs to simulate gas exhaustion. Expect a revert or design patterns like batching and then assert correct behavior. A common misconception is that testing vulnerabilities requires mainnet forks. In many cases you can fully exercise reentrancy and DoS logic on the local Hardhat network with crafted attacker contracts. The key takeaway: build tests that encode attack scenarios so they remain part of your regression suite and prevent reintroduction of these vulnerabilities. Testing for reentrancy and DoS means include attack simulations—malicious contracts and large-input scenarios—in your test suite to prove resistance to reentrancy and dos.. In practical terms, design adversarial tests that attempt to break your contract. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Adversarial testing
keyIdea.text: Include attack simulations—malicious contracts and large-input scenarios—in your test suite to prove resistance to reentrancy and DoS.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Vulnerability tests
Reentrancy test pattern
  • Deploy victim and attacker contracts in test setup.
  • Fund the victim with Ether, trigger the attack, then assert final balances or state.
  • If attack succeeds, the test demonstrates a vulnerability to be fixed.
Warning
If an adversarial test passes (attack succeeds), treat that as a high-priority security failure to remediate before deployment.
Denial-of-Service pattern
Construct tests that populate large arrays or trigger loops with many participants, and assert whether functions revert or handle batching correctly.
Key Takeaway
Adversarial tests serve as permanent regression checks against serious classes of vulnerabilities.

screens.title: Access control and revert testing
screens.subtitle: Assert that unauthorized calls fail and owners succeed

narration.text: Access control mistakes are common and often severe. Testing access controls requires explicit tests that attempt protected calls from unauthorized signers and expect reverts. For example, for an onlyOwner modifier you should deploy the contract with the owner signer, then connect a non-owner signer and assert the protected function reverts with the expected message. Also include a positive test where the owner calls the function successfully. This contrast ensures both sides of the access rule are covered. A common mistake is only writing the positive owner test and forgetting the unauthorized case; that leaves privilege escalation bugs undetected. Another point is to check for correct revert messages where your contract uses custom error strings. Use revertedWith when you want to assert a specific message and prefer a generic reverted assertion when relying on native checks. The key takeaway is to write complementary tests: one asserting success by the owner, and one asserting failure by a non-owner, so the contract’s authorization rules are fully exercised. Access control and revert testing means always test both authorized success and unauthorized failure to ensure modifiers enforce intended restrictions.. In practical terms, assert that unauthorized calls fail and owners succeed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Access control tests
keyIdea.text: Always test both authorized success and unauthorized failure to ensure modifiers enforce intended restrictions.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Access control
Failing authorization test
await expect(myContract.connect(addr1).onlyOwnerFunction())
  .to.be.revertedWith("Not owner");
Use revertedWith to assert specific error messages for clearer failure diagnostics, but a plain reverted check can be appropriate for native arithmetic failures.
Complementary success test
Also include a test where the owner calls the function and it returns the expected value or emits the expected event. This completes the authorization contract test.
Key Takeaway
Testing both failure and success cases validates access control and prevents privilege regressions.

screens.title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) for smart contracts
screens.subtitle: Write failing tests first to drive safer contract design

narration.text: Test-Driven Development is a practice where you write a test that fails, then write the smallest amount of code to make it pass, and finally refactor while keeping tests green. For smart contracts this discipline forces you to think about desired behavior and edge cases before implementing logic, which often results in smaller, more modular functions and clearer access controls. For example, write a failing test for an onlyOwner withdrawal: the test should assert that a non-owner cannot withdraw and that the owner can. Then implement the modifier and withdrawal logic to satisfy the test. Another concrete benefit is that TDD makes it easier to design functions that are testable and less gas-intensive, because you only add complexity to satisfy a failing test. A common misconception is that TDD slows development; in practice it reduces debugging time by preventing classes of bugs from being written in the first place. Key takeaway: use tests as design guides—start tests before code and keep them in the repo as living documentation of expected behavior. Test-Driven Development (TDD) for smart contracts means writing tests first guides contract design, surfaces edge cases early, and creates a regression suite to protect future refactors.. In practical terms, write failing tests first to drive safer contract design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: TDD value
keyIdea.text: Writing tests first guides contract design, surfaces edge cases early, and creates a regression suite to protect future refactors.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › TDD
TDD cycle
  1. Write a failing test that describes desired behavior.
  2. Implement the minimal code to pass the test.
  3. Refactor code while keeping tests green.
Example
Write a failing withdraw test, implement withdraw, then refactor for gas efficiency while test ensures behavior remains correct.
Why it matters
TDD prevents spec drift, makes expected behavior explicit, and produces tests that function as both design and safety checks for future changes.
Key Takeaway
Start tests before code to design safer contracts and preserve behavior through refactors.

screens.title: Common mistakes and test best practices
screens.subtitle: Improve coverage, avoid fragile tests, and plan for gas effects

narration.text: Knowing common mistakes helps you write stronger tests. One frequent error is insufficient coverage: only testing happy paths and neglecting edge cases like zero values, empty arrays, or unauthorized callers. Another is order-dependent tests caused by shared state; fix this by deploying fresh instances in beforeEach. Over-reliance on console logs instead of assertions is also common: a test that only prints values does not provide automated guarantees. Gas-related mistakes occur when you assume unbounded loops will behave the same on testnets and mainnet; write DoS tests that simulate large inputs and consider batching. Finally, ignoring event assertions can break integrations that rely on logs; always test events when they represent important signals. Best practices include using Waffle's expressive matchers, keeping tests focused and small, combining event and balance assertions for side effects, and adding adversarial tests to your regression suite. The result is a durable test suite that protects contract behavior and acts as living documentation for future contributors. Common mistakes and test best practices means write focused, isolated tests that assert behavior, cover edge cases, and include gas and adversarial scenarios to avoid fragile suites.. keyIdea.title: Avoid fragility
keyIdea.text: Write focused, isolated tests that assert behavior, cover edge cases, and include gas and adversarial scenarios to avoid fragile suites.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.4 › Mistakes & practices
Common mistakes
  • Only testing happy paths and ignoring edge cases.
  • Using shared state across tests causing order-dependence.
  • Relying on logs instead of automated assertions.
  • Ignoring gas considerations and DoS scenarios.
Best practices
  • Isolate tests with beforeEach deployments.
  • Assert events and state or balances together.
  • Add adversarial and large-input tests for security.
  • Measure coverage and include edge cases in test plans.
Key Takeaway
A disciplined test suite with edge-case coverage is a reliable defense against both logic bugs and attack vectors.
